issue.title: gh skill: add a minimum release age option to install/update (supply chain safety)

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: a request to improve CLI

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh skill command

issue.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

Without an explicit version or pin, `gh skill install` and `gh skill update` resolve to the newest version of a skill:
1. the latest GitHub release (`releases/latest`), or
2. the default branch HEAD if the repository has no release.

A skill that was published a few minutes ago (or a compromised release or commit) is therefore installed or updated immediately. Skills are executable-adjacent content: `SKILL.md` instructions and bundled `scripts/` are loaded by coding agents (Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, Codex, etc.) and can influence what the agent runs on the user's machine. A configurable delay would give maintainers and the community more time to detect and respond to compromised versions before users adopt them.

Today the only mitigation is to pin manually with `--pin <tag|SHA>` or `skill@version`. That requires vetting a specific version by hand, and pinned skills are skipped by `gh skill update` unless `--unpin` is used. There is no way to say "track the newest version, but only if it has been public for at least N days", which is a common policy in dependency managers.

### Proposed solution

Add a minimum age option to `gh skill install` and `gh skill update`, for example:

```shell
# Only consider versions published at least 7 days ago
gh skill install github/awesome-copilot git-commit --min-release-age 7d

# Update to the newest version that is at least 3 days old
gh skill update --all --min-release-age 3d
```

Suggested behavior:

- **Releases**: pick the newest release whose publish time (`published_at`) is at least the given age in the past. If the newest release is too young, fall back to the previous eligible release.
- **Default branch fallback** (repositories without releases): never silently bypass the age policy by installing HEAD. Author/committer dates do not establish publication time: they can be backdated, and they can also be old for legitimate reasons (for example a commit made weeks ago and pushed or fast-forwarded today). The repository activity API (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/activity`) may provide a basis for server-recorded timing, but history availability and the handling of force pushes, reverts, and branch deletion need investigation (for example, a past tip that was later removed by a force push should not be selected). If an eligible revision cannot be established safely, stop with a clear message. Refusing default-branch installs while this option is enabled would be a reasonable first version.
- **`update`**: do nothing if the installed skill is already at or newer than the eligible version, and never downgrade because of this option. Report skills that were skipped because the latest version is too young (this would also show up in `--dry-run`).
- **Explicit pins**: `--pin` and `skill@version` bypass the check, because the user chose that version explicitly. (Applying the check to explicit pins as well is defensible, so this is an open question.)
- **Configuration**: allow a persistent default through `gh config` and/or an environment variable, so users and CI do not have to repeat the flag. A flag-only first version would already be useful.
- **Duration format**: accept Go-style durations or days (`72h`, `7d`).

### Additional context

Other tools offer the same safeguard: pnpm `minimumReleaseAge`, uv `exclude-newer`, npm `--before`, and Renovate `minimumReleaseAge`.

A similar request exists for the Vercel skills CLI, which has the same exposure (new commits are picked up on the next `add`/`update`): vercel-labs/skills#2649. Since the two tools are intended to share a compatible lock format (see #14895), it would be good to keep the semantics of this option aligned where possible, e.g. whether an explicit pin bypasses the check.

Related, but not duplicates:
- #13276 (tracking upstream source for republished skills)
- #13215 (flags and contracts for automation-ready `gh skill`). A non-interactive `update --all --min-release-age` would fit well with session-start sync scripts.

I searched open and closed issues in this repository for "release age", "cooldown", "supply chain", and similar terms and did not find an existing request. Tested on gh 2.103.3.

issue.title: `gh issue develop --name <existing-branch>` fails with "API returned empty branch name" instead of saying the branch already exists

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: Affects a small number of users or is largely cosmetic

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh issue command

issue.body:
### Describe the bug

When `--name` is a branch that already exists on the remote, `gh issue develop` fails with:

```
failed to create linked branch: API returned empty branch name
```

The message points at the API response, not the cause. The underlying `createLinkedBranch` mutation returns HTTP 200 with `{"data":{"createLinkedBranch":{"linkedBranch":null}}}` and no `errors`, and nothing is linked or created.

This is likely the real cause behind #13805, which was closed without a reproduction: that report blamed the slash in the branch name, but the test below shows an existing branch fails with or without a slash, and a new branch with a slash works.

### Affected version

gh version 2.92.0 (2026-04-28), Linux

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. In any repository, push two branches: `example` and `feat/example`.
2. Open an issue.
3. Run `gh issue develop <issue> --repo <owner>/<repo> --name example --base example`.
4. See `failed to create linked branch: API returned empty branch name`. `gh issue develop --list <issue>` shows nothing linked.
5. Repeat with `--name feat/example --base feat/example`: same error.
6. Run `gh issue develop <issue> --repo <owner>/<repo> --name feat/new-example --base main`: the branch is created and linked.

### Tested

Private repository, gh 2.92.0, every branch pointing at the same `main` commit:

| Branch passed to `--name` | Already on remote? | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `example` | yes | `API returned empty branch name`, exit 1, nothing linked |
| `feat/example` | yes | `API returned empty branch name`, exit 1, nothing linked |
| `feat/new-example` | no | branch created and linked (`--list` shows it) |

Request ID of a failing mutation (from `GH_DEBUG=api`): `DB0E:26CBEE:1EB28F1:2CA6176:6AEC648D`

The third run was made outside a git checkout, so it also exited 1 with `fatal: not in a git directory` after creating the branch; that is #14856.

### Expected vs actual behavior

Expected: before calling `createLinkedBranch`, check whether the branch already exists and say so, for example "branch example already exists; the API can only link a new branch. Link it from the issue's Development sidebar." Or check for a `null` `linkedBranch` and explain it.

Actual: a generic "empty branch name" error.

### Additional context

The API side (no way to link an existing branch, and the silent `null`) is reported in https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/212130.

The check contexts of a pull request are paginated, so `gh` makes a second request for the remaining contexts. The second response is read without checking that the pull request it refers to is still there, which produces either a nil pointer dereference or an index out of range error.

```
gh version 2.103.3-71-g736c68f67 (2026-11-07)
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/latest
```

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Open a pull request that has more than 100 status checks, for example one that runs a large CI matrix.

3. Run:

   ```
   gh pr view <number>
   ```

4. View the output
5. See error

The crash also happens if the pull request still resolves but the list of commits comes back empty, which gives an index out of range error instead of a nil pointer dereference.

`gh pr view --json statusCheckRollup` reaches the same code.

labels.description: a request to improve CLI

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh auth command

issue.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

The new expiring credentials are a welcome improvement. GitHub documents an **eight-hour lifetime** for the resulting OAuth access token, however, and I’d like the option to use a shorter lifetime.

A local script or tool can obtain the current bearer token using `gh auth token`. Depending on when it obtains the token, a copied token may remain usable for much of its eight-hour lifetime, with the permissions granted to the CLI credential. A 15- or 60-minute lifetime could reduce the exposure window for an access-token-only leak.

### Proposed solution

Allow users or organizations to request a shorter, **server-enforced access-token lifetime** for GitHub CLI OAuth credentials, while continuing to use the refresh token for normal CLI operation.

Users could choose from a small set of lifetimes, or an organization could define an upper bound. The exact values and defaults could be determined by GitHub.

Shorter lifetimes would increase refresh frequency and could affect rate limits, concurrency, offline workflows, and tools that cache `gh auth token` output. They would reduce the useful lifetime of a stolen access token, but would not address theft of the refresh token or ongoing malicious code execution on the endpoint.

I understand the OAuth server determines the token’s actual expiration, and I could not find a documented way for `gh` to request a shorter lifetime today. Could the OAuth platform support this, and could `gh` expose it if available?

### Additional context

A client-side decision to stop using a token earlier would not invalidate an already copied token on GitHub. Narrower scopes and repository access would further reduce impact, but are separate from this lifetime request.

- [[GitHub OAuth: expiring access tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps#expiring-access-tokens)](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps#expiring-access-tokens)
- [[GitHub CLI expiring credentials announcement](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-21-github-cli-opt-in-to-expiring-auto-refreshing-oauth-tokens/)](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-21-github-cli-opt-in-to-expiring-auto-refreshing-oauth-tokens/)

issue.title: gh auth git-credential get fails (exit 1) when Git passes username=<account> for a logged-in non-active account

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: this is already captured in another issue

issue.body:
### Describe the bug

When multiple accounts are authenticated on `github.com` in GitHub CLI (for example, an Enterprise Managed User `<user>_<org>` and a personal account `<personal-user>`), `gh auth switch` toggles a single global active account across all terminals.

Even when a repository or Git configuration explicitly specifies the expected account (`credential.https://github.com.username=<personal-user>` or `https://<personal-user>@github.com/...`), `gh auth git-credential get` rejects `username=<personal-user>` and exits with code `1` whenever a different account is globally active.

In non-interactive environments (such as IDE agent hosts or automation runners that pass `git -c credential.interactive=never`), Git then falls through to the system credential manager and fails with:
```text
fatal: Cannot prompt because user interactivity has been disabled.
fatal: unable to get password from user
```

### Affected version

- `gh version 2.103.3 (2026-10-26)`
- `git version 2.56.0.windows.4` (Windows x64)

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Authenticate two accounts on `github.com` (`<account-a>` and `<account-b>`) in `gh`.
2. Set `<account-a>` as the active account:
   ```sh
   gh auth switch --hostname github.com --user <account-a>
   ```
3. Invoke `gh auth git-credential get` with `username=<account-b>`:
   ```text
   protocol=https
   host=github.com
   username=<account-b>
   ```
4. Observe that `gh auth git-credential get` exits with code `1` and returns no credentials, even though `<account-b>` has a valid token in the keyring (`gh auth token --hostname github.com --user <account-b>` succeeds).

### Expected vs actual behavior

- **Expected:** When Git passes `username=<account-b>` to `gh auth git-credential get` and `<account-b>` is an authenticated account for `host` in `gh`, `gh auth git-credential` should resolve and return `<account-b>`'s token from the keyring (rather than requiring global `gh auth switch` state to match or requiring a per-repo `!GH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token -h github.com -u <account-b>) gh auth git-credential` helper).
- **Actual:** `gh auth git-credential get` only checks the globally active account for the host and exits `1` when `username` does not match the active account.

labels.description: relating to the gh extension command

issue.body:
### Describe the bug

On Apple Silicon, `gh extension install` / `upgrade` always re-signs a downloaded `darwin-arm64` extension binary ad-hoc, even when the binary is already validly signed with a Developer ID (`pkg/cmd/extension/manager.go`, `codesignBinary`):

```go
codesign --sign - --force --preserve-metadata=entitlements,requirements,flags,runtime <binPath>
```

Because `requirements` is preserved, the installed binary keeps the Developer ID *designated requirement* but now carries an ad-hoc signature, so it no longer satisfies its own designated requirement:

```
$ codesign -d -r- ~/.local/share/gh/extensions/gh-sk/gh-sk
designated => identifier "io.github.kezhenxu94.gh-sk" and anchor apple generic and certificate 1[field.1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.6] /* exists */ and certificate leaf[field.1.2.840.113635.100.6.1.13] /* exists */ and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = "58JAK95Y3A"
$ codesign --verify --strict --verbose=2 ~/.local/share/gh/extensions/gh-sk/gh-sk
.../gh-sk: valid on disk
.../gh-sk: does not satisfy its designated Requirement
```

This breaks anything that relies on code identity. For example, an extension that reads the macOS Keychain: "Always Allow" records the designated requirement, which the binary can never satisfy, so macOS prompts for the login password on **every** keychain read. It also makes it impossible for extension authors to ship a stable signing identity across releases (the reason to sign with a Developer ID in the first place).

### Affected version

```
gh version 2.95.0 (2026-06-17)
```

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Publish a `darwin-arm64` release asset signed with a Developer ID (`codesign --sign "Developer ID Application: …" --identifier <id> --timestamp --options runtime`). `codesign --verify --strict` passes on the asset.
2. On an Apple Silicon Mac: `gh extension install <owner>/<repo>`.
3. `codesign --verify --strict --verbose=2 ~/.local/share/gh/extensions/<name>/<name>` reports `does not satisfy its designated Requirement`, and `codesign -dv` shows `Signature=adhoc`.

Example: https://github.com/kezhenxu94/gh-sk/releases/tag/v0.4.1 (both assets verify as Developer ID, team `58JAK95Y3A`, before install).

### Expected vs actual behavior

Expected: a binary that already has a valid signature (`codesign --verify --strict` succeeds) is installed unchanged; ad-hoc signing is only applied to unsigned binaries, which is what it is needed for.

Actual: every `darwin-arm64` binary is re-signed ad-hoc while keeping its old requirements, leaving validly signed binaries with an unsatisfiable designated requirement.

A possible fix: in `codesignBinary`, skip re-signing when `codesign --verify --strict <binPath>` succeeds (or at least drop `requirements` from `--preserve-metadata` so the result is self-consistent).

### Logs

N/A (no error is reported; the problem is the resulting signature).

issue.title: Preserve literal Unicode escape text in JSON string values

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: Affects a small number of users or is largely cosmetic

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh api command

issue.body:
## Summary

JSON response sanitization changes literal backslash-u text inside a string value, even when that value contains no terminal control character. This silently changes issue body content returned by `gh api` and `gh issue view --json body`. A valid JSON example stored inside a Markdown body can become invalid after readback. The outer API response remains valid JSON; this report concerns its changed string value, not a failure to parse that outer response.

## Steps to reproduce

Run the following Python 3 script with the tested release on `PATH`. It serves only a local fixture, uses an isolated configuration directory and a dummy token, and creates no GitHub resource. The `body` field contains a JSON string example made of ordinary printable text; `control` separately contains an actual ESC character as a sanitization control.

```python
import http.server
import json
import os
import subprocess
import tempfile
import threading

fixture = {"body": '"\\u001b[31mexample"', "control": "\x1b[31mexample", "plain": "example"}
payload = json.dumps(fixture).encode()

class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(payload)
    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass

server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
thread = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
thread.start()
try:
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as config:
        env = {k: v for k, v in os.environ.items() if not k.startswith(("GH_", "GITHUB_"))}
        env.update(GH_CONFIG_DIR=config, GH_TOKEN="local-fixture-placeholder", NO_COLOR="1")
        result = subprocess.run(["gh", "api", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/fixture"], env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        actual = json.loads(result.stdout)
        print("input:", repr(fixture["body"]))
        print("output:", repr(actual["body"]))
        print("body equal:", actual["body"] == fixture["body"])
        print("actual ESC neutralized:", actual["control"] == "^[[31mexample")
        print("plain unchanged:", actual["plain"] == fixture["plain"])
        json.loads(fixture["body"])
        try:
            json.loads(actual["body"])
        except json.JSONDecodeError as error:
            print("embedded JSON:", error.msg)
finally:
    server.shutdown()
    server.server_close()
    thread.join()
```

The fixture was reduced from a public issue body and executed locally. The same failure was also reproduced by fetching the existing issue through both affected commands and comparing its decoded body with a direct REST response. No issue write is necessary to reproduce it.

## Expected behavior

Preserve literal `\u001b` text that is already escaped in the outer JSON string. Decoding that outer string produces printable backslash-u notation, not an ESC character. Keep neutralizing actual control characters, as demonstrated by the separate `control` field.

This distinction matches the [review requirement on the original sanitization change](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/6916#issuecomment-1409101560): already escaped Unicode codepoints should remain unchanged. It also matches the sanitizer's stated scope: bytes that are not part of a control character are not modified. This report does not assume that `gh api` generally bypasses sanitization or preserves the entire wire response byte for byte.

## Actual behavior

Both the installed executable and a separately downloaded official release executable produced the following result with stdout captured through a pipe and color disabled. Each command exited successfully. The source body and its embedded JSON parse successfully; the returned body's embedded JSON does not.

```text
input: '"\\u001b[31mexample"'
output: '"\\^[[31mexample"'
body equal: False
actual ESC neutralized: True
plain unchanged: True
embedded JSON: Invalid \escape
```

The two `repr` lines above display a Python representation of the strings. The replacement leaves a literal backslash before caret notation. Adding `--allow-escape-sequences` did not preserve the value, and `--jq .body` returned the same changed text. Actual ESC sanitization and ordinary text preservation both passed the controls.

## Evidence

- Expected source: The original change's review requirement linked above and [`asciisanitizer.Sanitizer.Transform`'s documented scope](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/asciisanitizer/sanitizer.go#L27-L29) distinguish actual control characters from other bytes.
- Failure source: The executed self-contained fixture and output above, reproduced with both release executables; an independent live REST comparison also showed five literal escape tokens changed in a stored issue body while GitHub retained the original content.
- Evidence provenance: observed
- Local verification: reproduced
- Reproduction completeness: complete

The HTTP response path applies the [JSON sanitizer to application/json responses](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/api/http_client.go#L259-L273). The [matching branch](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/asciisanitizer/sanitizer.go#L69-L94) recognizes the six-byte escape pattern even after an escaped backslash. Its extra-backslash handling keeps the outer JSON valid, but still changes the decoded literal text. This is a source explanation, not a prescribed implementation.

There is counterevidence worth making explicit: the current [sanitizer test](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/asciisanitizer/sanitizer_test.go#L24-L29) and the CLI's [HTTP client test](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/eeb44bc432c0107de002dadd34a61b4e2bd15882/api/http_client_test.go#L431-L471) encode the existing replacement for escaped patterns. They protect outer-JSON validity but do not preserve the printable literal value. The narrower failure here is the content change demonstrated above, rather than a request to remove control-character protection.

## Restoration check

With the same fixture, the returned `body` must equal the input `body`, and `json.loads(actual["body"])` must succeed as it does for the input. The `control` field must still contain caret notation rather than an actual ESC character, and `plain` must remain unchanged. Check both direct API output and issue-body structured output so that a passing outer JSON parse alone cannot hide the content change.

## Runtime or environment

- Runtime-tested: GitHub CLI 2.103.3 on macOS arm64, both the installed Mach-O executable and the official macOS arm64 release archive; the archive's SHA-256 matched the published checksums. All output was captured without a TTY.
- Source-inspected, not built: current default branch `trunk` at `eeb44bc432c0107de002dadd34a61b4e2bd15882`; the HTTP client and its sanitization tests are unchanged from the release. Both pin `github.com/cli/go-gh/v2 v2.17.0`, which was also the library's latest published release when checked.

## References

- [Closed issue #8336](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/8336) concerned invalid outer JSON causing issue view to fail; its fix restored parseability. This report reproduces changed string content while the outer response remains parseable.
- [Closed issue #14545](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/14545) was not reproduced and was closed requesting exact current reproduction; it alleged backslash loss and invalid outer JSON. This report provides a current local fixture for a different observable result and makes no user-agent-dependent or reserialization claim.

## Triage assessment

- Impact level: P2
- Assessment status: supported
- Impact basis: Structured readback silently changes valid literal source text, making an embedded JSON example invalid and preventing exact issue-body verification; the observed scope is strings containing escaped control-code notation.
- Workaround status: available
- Workaround basis: A direct REST request using Python urllib preserved the decoded issue body and its valid embedded example in the live comparison; this avoids the CLI response sanitizer without changing the stored issue or weakening terminal protection in gh.

issue.title: gh extension upgrade shows no progress for a long time, indistinguishable from a hang

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: a request to improve CLI

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh extension command

issue.body:
### Describe the bug

`gh extension upgrade <name>` prints only the `[<name>]:` prefix and then shows nothing else, with no spinner, progress text or status, for a long time (about 40 seconds on a second attempt). While this is happening there is no way to tell whether the upgrade is working (downloading the release asset) or is stuck. On the first attempt I assumed it was hung and interrupted it with Ctrl+C after about 14 seconds. On the second attempt the same command finished on its own after about 42 seconds and printed the result.

### Affected version

```
gh version 2.103.3 (2026-10-26)
```

Extension being upgraded: a precompiled binary extension, `github/gh-stack`, from v0.2.1 to v0.3.0. Linux, installed extension was not pinned.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Have a binary extension installed that has a newer release available. The extension itself printed "A new release is available: 0.2.1 -> 0.3.0. To upgrade, run: gh extension upgrade stack".
2. Run `gh extension upgrade stack`.
3. The terminal shows only `[stack]:` and then nothing.

### Expected vs actual behavior

Expected: some indication of progress while the upgrade runs, for example "checking for updates...", "downloading v0.3.0...", and then the result, so the user can tell it is working and not hung.

Actual: only `[stack]:` is printed, followed by silence for tens of seconds, and then the result line appears at the end. The empty prefix looks identical to a hang, so users are likely to cancel a working upgrade. Cancelling may also leave the upgrade in an unknown state.

### Logs

First attempt, interrupted by me after about 14 seconds:

```
$ gh extension upgrade stack
[stack]:


^C
```

Second attempt, which succeeded after about 42 seconds, with the prefix being the only output until the end:

```
$ gh extension upgrade stack
[stack]: upgraded from v0.2.1 to v0.3.0
✓ Successfully checked extension upgrades
```

Running it a third time afterwards returned immediately with `[stack]: already up to date`.

### Suggestion

Show a spinner or progress message while `gh extension upgrade` is checking for and downloading a release (at least when stdout is a TTY), and print the target version before the download starts. This is related to #6463, which asks for information about the changes when upgrading, but this issue is only about showing progress and status so a slow upgrade can be told apart from a stuck one.

issue.title: Preserve literal Unicode escape text in JSON string values

labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: Affects a small number of users or is largely cosmetic

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh api command

issue.body:
## Summary

JSON response sanitization changes literal backslash-u text inside a string value, even when that value contains no terminal control character. This silently changes issue body content returned by `gh api` and `gh issue view --json body`. A valid JSON example stored inside a Markdown body can become invalid after readback. The outer API response remains valid JSON; this report concerns its changed string value, not a failure to parse that outer response.

## Steps to reproduce

Run the following Python 3 script with the tested release on `PATH`. It serves only a local fixture, uses an isolated configuration directory and a dummy token, and creates no GitHub resource. The `body` field contains a JSON string example made of ordinary printable text; `control` separately contains an actual ESC character as a sanitization control.

```python
import http.server
import json
import os
import subprocess
import tempfile
import threading

fixture = {"body": '"\\u001b[31mexample"', "control": "\x1b[31mexample", "plain": "example"}
payload = json.dumps(fixture).encode()

class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(payload)
    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass

server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
thread = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
thread.start()
try:
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as config:
        env = {k: v for k, v in os.environ.items() if not k.startswith(("GH_", "GITHUB_"))}
        env.update(GH_CONFIG_DIR=config, GH_TOKEN="local-fixture-placeholder", NO_COLOR="1")
        result = subprocess.run(["gh", "api", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/fixture"], env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        actual = json.loads(result.stdout)
        print("input:", repr(fixture["body"]))
        print("output:", repr(actual["body"]))
        print("body equal:", actual["body"] == fixture["body"])
        print("actual ESC neutralized:", actual["control"] == "^[[31mexample")
        print("plain unchanged:", actual["plain"] == fixture["plain"])
        json.loads(fixture["body"])
        try:
            json.loads(actual["body"])
        except json.JSONDecodeError as error:
            print("embedded JSON:", error.msg)
finally:
    server.shutdown()
    server.server_close()
    thread.join()
```

The fixture was reduced from a public issue body and executed locally. The same failure was also reproduced by fetching the existing issue through both affected commands and comparing its decoded body with a direct REST response. No issue write is necessary to reproduce it.

## Expected behavior

Preserve literal `\u001b` text that is already escaped in the outer JSON string. Decoding that outer string produces printable backslash-u notation, not an ESC character. Keep neutralizing actual control characters, as demonstrated by the separate `control` field.

This distinction matches the [review requirement on the original sanitization change](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/6916#issuecomment-1409101560): already escaped Unicode codepoints should remain unchanged. It also matches the sanitizer's stated scope: bytes that are not part of a control character are not modified. This report does not assume that `gh api` generally bypasses sanitization or preserves the entire wire response byte for byte.

## Actual behavior

Both the installed executable and a separately downloaded official release executable produced the following result with stdout captured through a pipe and color disabled. Each command exited successfully. The source body and its embedded JSON parse successfully; the returned body's embedded JSON does not.

```text
input: '"\\u001b[31mexample"'
output: '"\\^[[31mexample"'
body equal: False
actual ESC neutralized: True
plain unchanged: True
embedded JSON: Invalid \escape
```

The two `repr` lines above display a Python representation of the strings. The replacement leaves a literal backslash before caret notation. Adding `--allow-escape-sequences` did not preserve the value, and `--jq .body` returned the same changed text. Actual ESC sanitization and ordinary text preservation both passed the controls.

## Evidence

- Expected source: The original change's review requirement linked above and [`asciisanitizer.Sanitizer.Transform`'s documented scope](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/asciisanitizer/sanitizer.go#L27-L29) distinguish actual control characters from other bytes.
- Failure source: The executed self-contained fixture and output above, reproduced with both release executables; an independent live REST comparison also showed five literal escape tokens changed in a stored issue body while GitHub retained the original content.
- Evidence provenance: observed
- Local verification: reproduced
- Reproduction completeness: complete

The HTTP response path applies the [JSON sanitizer to application/json responses](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/api/http_client.go#L259-L273). The [matching branch](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/asciisanitizer/sanitizer.go#L69-L94) recognizes the six-byte escape pattern even after an escaped backslash. Its extra-backslash handling keeps the outer JSON valid, but still changes the decoded literal text. This is a source explanation, not a prescribed implementation.

There is counterevidence worth making explicit: the current [sanitizer test](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/asciisanitizer/sanitizer_test.go#L24-L29) and the CLI's [HTTP client test](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/eeb44bc432c0107de002dadd34a61b4e2bd15882/api/http_client_test.go#L431-L471) encode the existing replacement for escaped patterns. They protect outer-JSON validity but do not preserve the printable literal value. The narrower failure here is the content change demonstrated above, rather than a request to remove control-character protection.

## Restoration check

With the same fixture, the returned `body` must equal the input `body`, and `json.loads(actual["body"])` must succeed as it does for the input. The `control` field must still contain caret notation rather than an actual ESC character, and `plain` must remain unchanged. Check both direct API output and issue-body structured output so that a passing outer JSON parse alone cannot hide the content change.

## Runtime or environment

- Runtime-tested: GitHub CLI 2.103.3 on macOS arm64, both the installed Mach-O executable and the official macOS arm64 release archive; the archive's SHA-256 matched the published checksums. All output was captured without a TTY.
- Source-inspected, not built: current default branch `trunk` at `eeb44bc432c0107de002dadd34a61b4e2bd15882`; the HTTP client and its sanitization tests are unchanged from the release. Both pin `github.com/cli/go-gh/v2 v2.17.0`, which was also the library's latest published release when checked.

## References

- [Closed issue #14545](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/14545) was not reproduced and was closed requesting exact current reproduction; it alleged backslash loss and invalid outer JSON. labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: Affects a small number of users or is largely cosmetic

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh auth command

issue.body:
### Describe the bug

`gh auth login` (and `gh auth status`) hang indefinitely, with no output and no error, when the Secret Service provider is in a broken state. In my case there were two `gnome-keyring-daemon` instances on the session bus after the daemon crashed and was restarted.

Each attempt triggered a desktop keyring unlock prompt, which appeared twice. Then `gnome-keyring-daemon` crashed. `gh` never timed out or reported anything. When run from a terminal where the desktop prompt isn't visible, it just hangs, so the one-time device code and the URL are never shown.

After the crash, two daemons were running:

- `gnome-keyring-daemon --start --foreground --components=secrets`, D-Bus-activated (in `dbus.service`'s cgroup)
- `gnome-keyring-daemon --foreground --components=pkcs11,secrets --control-directory=...`, the systemd user unit `gnome-keyring-daemon.service`

Killing the D-Bus-activated instance and running `systemctl --user restart gnome-keyring-daemon.socket gnome-keyring-daemon.service` fixed it immediately. After a single keyring unlock, `gh auth login -w` worked normally.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

The trigger is environmental and hard to reproduce on purpose:

1. Have a GNOME session where `gnome-keyring-daemon` crashes and a second instance gets D-Bus-activated next to the systemd-managed one, so two Secret Service owners exist.
2. Have a stored token that is no longer valid (`gh auth status` reports "The token in default is invalid").
3. Run `gh auth login -h github.com -p ssh -w` or `gh auth status`.
4. `gh` blocks on the keyring call forever. No device code is printed, and there is no timeout or error.

### Expected vs actual behavior

**Expected:** if the keyring / Secret Service call doesn't return within a reasonable time, `gh` fails with an actionable message. For example: "the system keyring did not respond; unlock it, or retry with `--insecure-storage`". For `auth status`, at least report that the keyring is unresponsive.

**Actual:** an indefinite silent hang. `gh auth status` hangs the same way.

### Logs / environment

- gh version 2.103.1 (2026-10-23)
- Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, GNOME on Wayland
- gnome-keyring 50.0 (`gnome-keyring-daemon` crash report recorded by apport at the time)

### Related

- #7356: same symptom, where the cause was a keyring unlock prompt shown on the local desktop while `gh` waited silently.
- #13317: a different keyring failure mode (silent fallback to unauthenticated requests).

A timeout plus a hint about `--insecure-storage` would have turned this into a self-explanatory error instead of an apparent freeze.

issue.title: Add a way to get the output of check runs with `gh pr checks`.
issue.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve
`gh pr checks` shows the status of checks. But as far as I can tell there is no way to get the output of the checks (besides using `gh api` to make a request to the [check-runs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/runs?apiVersion=2026-03-10#list-check-runs-for-a-git-reference) endpoint). 

I want to be able to inspect the output, in particular the title and summary, and possibly the text. 

### Proposed solution

Add additional field for the check's output. Or alternatively, have some identifier for the check that can be used as a json field. And a new subcommand for fetching the output of a single check.

issue.title: Support optional Touch ID or user-presence protection for refreshable credentials on macOS

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: a request to improve CLI

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh auth command

issue.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

The new refreshable OAuth credentials reduce the lifetime of a leaked access token, but `gh` still needs to retain a refresh token that can obtain new credentials.

On macOS, `gh` uses Keychain through `zalando/go-keyring`. The CLI’s [[macOS Keyring Security notes](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/docs/macos-keyring.md)](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/docs/macos-keyring.md) explain that this invokes `/usr/bin/security` and that direct calls to `security` can also access stored `gh` tokens, subject to Keychain access controls. This makes the refresh credential an interesting target for malicious code running in a developer’s user session.

Could `gh` offer an **optional user-presence requirement**, such as Touch ID, to protect refreshable credentials?

### Proposed solution

Provide an opt-in macOS credential-storage mode that requires user presence before accessing the refresh token or performing a token refresh.

My preferred experience would be:

1. Use `gh` normally while the access token remains valid.
2. When the access token needs refreshing, prompt for Touch ID or an appropriate user-presence mechanism.
3. After approval, refresh and continue normally.
4. In non-interactive environments, fail with a clear message rather than hanging indefinitely.

This would give users a way to make access to the refresh credential require local user participation, while preserving normal CLI use between refreshes.

### Additional context

- Whether macOS Keychain APIs can provide this behavior for `gh`’s distribution model.
- Whether access and refresh credentials could be protected separately.
- How to support CLI extensions, headless sessions, and a configurable authentication reuse period.
- Whether another credential broker or platform-native mechanism would be a better fit.

Touch ID would be a local access-control improvement, not a guarantee that an extracted bearer token is device-bound. A process that obtains an access token after approval could still copy it.

### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

The new refreshable OAuth credentials reduce the lifetime of a leaked access token, but `gh` still needs to retain a refresh token that can obtain new credentials.

Could `gh` offer an **optional user-presence requirement**, such as Touch ID, to protect refreshable credentials?

### Proposed solution

Provide an opt-in macOS credential-storage mode that requires user presence before accessing the refresh token or performing a token refresh.

My preferred experience would be:

1. Use `gh` normally while the access token remains valid.
2. When the access token needs refreshing, prompt for Touch ID or an appropriate user-presence mechanism.
3. After approval, refresh and continue normally.
4. In non-interactive environments, fail with a clear message rather than hanging indefinitely.

An optional, bounded authentication reuse period could make this practical for frequent commands. The current behavior could remain available for unattended workflows.

This would give users a way to make access to the refresh credential require local user participation, while preserving normal CLI use between refreshes.

### Additional context

The current implementation stores access and refresh information together, so prompting only for refresh may require a different storage design. I also understand that changing the macOS Keychain integration has distribution and code-signing tradeoffs, including for Homebrew builds.

I’d appreciate maintainers’ thoughts on:

- Whether macOS Keychain APIs can provide this behavior for `gh`’s distribution model.
- Whether access and refresh credentials could be protected separately.
- How to support CLI extensions, headless sessions, and a configurable authentication reuse period.
- Whether another credential broker or platform-native mechanism would be a better fit.

Touch ID would be a local access-control improvement, not a guarantee that an extracted bearer token is device-bound. A process that obtains an access token after approval could still copy it.

issue.title: Allow a shorter Refresh Token inactiviy lifetime and document Incident Response revocation

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: a request to improve CLI

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh auth command

issue.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

Thank you for adding support for expiring, automatically refreshed credentials! This is a meaningful improvement over non-expiring access tokens.

GitHub documents that the refresh token expires after **six months without use**. Because a successful refresh rotates it, an actively used session can persist longer than six months. If the current refresh token is stolen, an attacker may be able to exchange it for a new token pair and continue refreshing it.

I’d be comfortable trading some convenience for a shorter inactivity window. For example, with a **10-day rolling inactivity limit**, my CLI would keep working after a few days away, but I’d need to sign in again after a two-week vacation.

There is also an incident-response question: if I suspect malware ran on my laptop and accessed the refreshable credential, I want to know precisely how to **revoke that credential server-side**, including if the attacker has already exchanged the stolen refresh token for a new pair.

### Proposed solution

**1. Support a shorter, server-enforced refresh-token inactivity lifetime.**

Allow a user or organization to request a shorter inactivity lifetime for GitHub CLI authentication. This would let users reduce the usable window for an unused stolen refresh token while retaining automatic refresh during normal use.

A separate absolute session lifetime could also be useful, but is not essential to this request.

A client-side timeout that deletes the local credential would improve local session hygiene, but it would not shorten the validity of a refresh token already copied by an attacker. Likewise, a rolling inactivity limit would not impose an absolute session limit if an attacker keeps using the credential.

I understand this lifetime appears to be controlled by GitHub’s OAuth platform, not by `gh` alone. Is there an existing platform capability for this? If not, could this request be routed to the appropriate team?

**2. Document the incident-response procedure for refreshable credentials.**

Please document how a user or security team should respond when they suspect the GitHub CLI access token **or refresh token** has been stolen, for example following a malware infection on a developer laptop.

In particular:

- Does revoking **GitHub CLI** under **Settings → Applications → Authorized OAuth Apps** invalidate the current refresh token and any token pair an attacker obtained through a prior refresh?
- Is there a supported way to revoke a **single device’s credential or token family**, rather than the GitHub CLI authorization across all devices?
- Is there an API-supported procedure for revoking an OAuth app refresh token when its value is known? Does it work if the token has already been rotated?
- What should responders expect from `gh` after revocation, and what evidence or security-log events, if any, can help investigate refresh-token theft or reuse?
- Could `gh auth logout` or the authentication documentation point users to the server-side revocation procedure and explain its scope?

I understand that `gh auth logout` removes local authentication configuration and does not itself revoke tokens. Clear guidance would help responders contain an incident without mistaking local cleanup for server-side revocation.

### Additional context

The GitHub CLI manual currently documents revoking the **GitHub CLI** OAuth app authorization and notes that this affects CLI authentication tokens across devices. More detail about rotating refresh tokens and incident response would be helpful.

A rejected refresh token could be a useful investigation signal if an attacker exchanged a stolen token before the legitimate CLI did. It would not, by itself, prove theft, and the absence of a failure would not rule out compromise.

- [[GitHub OAuth: expiring access tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps#expiring-access-tokens)](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps#expiring-access-tokens)

issue.title: Windows: api --input - reports unexpected end of JSON input from Python subprocess while file input works
issue.body:
> [!NOTE]
> 🤖 gpt-6.1-sol responding on behalf of Elliot

Observed on Windows PowerShell with Python 3.15 and the native gh.exe:

```python
payload = json.dumps({"body": "an ASCII-only review reply"})
subprocess.run(["gh", "api", endpoint, "--input", "-"], input=payload,
               text=True, capture_output=True)
```

Valid JSON passed through this subprocess stdin path repeatedly exits 1 with empty stdout and `unexpected end of JSON input`. No reply is created. Writing the same serialized payload as UTF-8 without BOM and passing its path to `--input` succeeds and the created reply can be read back. Authenticated reads and file-backed writes work with the same executable/account. Root cause (CLI versus Windows/Python stdin handling) is not established; the error does not identify where the input was lost.

Expected: consume the supplied JSON or provide a diagnostic that identifies the empty/truncated input source.

Version:
```
gh version 2.100.0 (2026-09-03)
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.100.0
```

comment.body: Thanks @ElliotDrel. I'm going to close this issue since this isn't reproducible and sounds like the underlying issue is that your environment is tainting github API responses somehow.

issue.title: gh loads user32.dll on every start on Windows because of atotto/clipboard

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: a request to improve CLI

issue.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

On Windows every gh process loads user32.dll, and with it win32u, gdi32, gdi32full and imm32, including `gh --version` and `gh api`. gh does not use them outside of copying the one-time code during login. They are loaded by `github.com/atotto/clipboard` v0.1.4 (imported by `internal/authflow`): its `clipboard_windows.go` calls `syscall.MustLoadDLL("user32")` and `MustFindProc` at package initialization, so the DLL is loaded before `main` runs.

atotto/clipboard#74 (open) changes these to lazy `windows.NewLazySystemDLL` lookups.

Measurements: gh 2.103.3 built twice with Go 1.27.3 and the release ldflags, once as is and once with `replace github.com/atotto/clipboard => <v0.1.4 + #74>`. Windows 11, interleaved runs, median of paired differences with 95% confidence interval, two separate runs:

| | images loaded | `gh --version` | `gh api /user` (local test server) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| as is | 16 | | |
| with #74 | 10 | -4.1 ms (2.7 to 5.4); -7.5 ms (5.4 to 11.4) | -1.6 ms (-1.1 to 4.2); -3.5 ms (0.4 to 5.2) |

The self-built gh matches the release binary. Reading the clipboard still works with the lazy version (checked in a small test program).

### Proposed solution

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: a request to improve CLI

labels.name: repo-5551e398
labels.description: relating to the gh pr command

issue.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

Add a --json response object with the ability to chain a jq query.

### Proposed solution

This will avoid doing something like this to get the id or other metadata of a PR we just created:

```bash
PR_URL=$(gh pr \
  create \
  --base main \
  --head develop \
  --title "Promote dev to main" \
  --body "Automated promotion PR from dev to main" \
  --fill \
  | tail -n1)

PR_NUMBER=$(basename "$PR_URL")
```

And instead make it possible to do this:

```bash
PR_NUMBER=$(gh pr \
  create \
  --base main \
  --head develop \
  --title "Promote dev to main" \
  --body "Automated promotion PR from dev to main" \
  --json number,url \
  --jq '.[0].number'
)
```

Or this:

```bash
PR_NUMBER=$(gh pr \
  create \
  --base main \
  --head develop \
  --title "Promote dev to main" \
  --body "Automated promotion PR from dev to main" \
  --json number,url
)

PR_URL=$(echo "$PR_JSON" | jq -r '.[0].url')
PR_NUMBER=$(echo "$PR_JSON" | jq -r '.[0].number')
```

### Additional context

Also, this would improve CLI API consistency

pinned_comment.body:
Fair enough. Here's the A/C for this issue.

## Acceptance Criteria

#### Interactive flow

**Given** I have a branch checked out and have it pushed to the remote repo
**When** I run `pr create --json id,url,number`, follow the prompts **(interactive flow)**
**Then** A PR is created, and I see a JSON on stdout with the `url`, `id` and `number` fields of the created PR

#### Non-interactive flow

**Given** I have a branch checked out and have it pushed to the remote repo
**When** I run `pr create --json id,url,number --title foo --body bar 2>/dev/null | cat` **(non-interactive flow)**
**Then** I see a JSON on stdout with the `url`, `id` and `number` fields of the created PR

#### JQ support

**Given** I have a branch checked out and have it pushed to the remote repo
**When** I run `pr create --json id,url,number --jq .number --title foo --body bar 2>/dev/null | cat`
**Then** I see the PR number is printed on stdout

#### Incompatible with `--dry-run`

**When** I run `pr create --json id --dry-run`
**Then** I get an error message saying these options are mutually exclusive

#### Independent of `--template`

**Given** My repo has a PR template named `pull_request_template.md`
**When** I run `pr create --json id,url,number --template pull_request_template.md`
**Then**  I see a JSON on stdout with the `url`, `id` and `number` fields of the created PR, **AND** the PR is created off of the given template

comment.body:
Hey @ElliotDrel 👋 Thanks for the detailed report, and for comparing piped and file input.

TLDR - I think something between `gh` and GitHub is answering the piped request with an empty error. `gh` then hides the real HTTP status, which is #10579.

Your file workaround is the way to go for now. Letting `gh` build the body from fields also avoids stdin:

```shell
# Pass the payload as a file path instead of "-"
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/NUMBER/comments/COMMENT_ID/replies --input payload.json

# Or let gh build the JSON body from fields
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/NUMBER/comments/COMMENT_ID/replies -f body='an ASCII-only review reply'
```

Here's what points to something in between:

- `unexpected end of JSON input` means `gh` got an error response with an empty body. It isn't about the JSON you sent.
- Piped and file input differ in one way. Piped requests have no `Content-Length` header because `gh` streams the body.
- GitHub handled piped input fine in my testing. Empty, cut-off, stalled, chunked, and 600 KB bodies all got readable errors on macOS with `gh` 2.102.1.

It could be a proxy, antivirus HTTPS scanning, or an agent sandbox's network proxy. If you can share the output of the failing call with `GH_DEBUG=api` set, the response status and headers should show what answered. `gh` redacts your token, but please double-check before posting.

- #10579
- #5820
- [Another Windows and Python report of this error with `--input -`, worked around with a temp file](https://github.com/makhammadsoliyev/Anjeer/commit/a4e7df7f4b)

+# Prepares ghmock for the issue-triage agent, which runs gh builds against it

+# and downloads GitHub's schemas.

+# so nothing the agent runs, including a gh alias or extension, can replace a

+#

+#   GHMOCK_GRAPHQL_SCHEMA, GHMOCK_REST_SCHEMA

issue.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

For security reasons and In corporates especially, it is very important to access the gh token in a secured way
We work with 1Password for keeping all secrets, including gh auth token

This way it is not possible to get the token freely when it is saved in the keychain, and any plugin of VScode or any code running on the machine can get it.
We tested it: we already wrote a "malicious" plugin in VS Code that freely ran gh auth token, stole it and stole all the code available, and even pushed the malicious code to where possible in PRs 
This way, IMHO all code of the GitHub itself was stolen and many other companies and open-source projects' code.

We must assume that the attacker is already on our computer, and protect all we have before it can make problems, and until the threat is deleted
That is why we moved to 1Password, and nothing, absolutely nothing, is kept in the way it can be easily accessed, like: gh auth token, that can be ran from any place by an attacker (for cli, vs code, whatever)  

The gh token rotation is good, very good, we waited for it
Now if the token is stolen and copied to another computer, that time till expire it.
But it is not enough protection in our days
Keeping the token, even rotated, in free accessible way in the keyring; or keychain, with "gh auth token"  extracted from anywhere, is not acceptable in our days and of course, not in security companies or big enterprises that use GitHub
### Proposed solution

We already starting using 1Password: gh auth login --op
As an additional way to keep token, in addition to keychain, keyrign and windows store
https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/14908

Rotated token is saved in 1Password, and all operations I do 
gh copilot
gh pr
git push
vim copilot 

Asks me to get the token from 1Password with fingerprint protection

How will it benefit CLI and its users?
It will protect the best way each CLI users from any possible attack, even on their computers

issue.body:
> [!NOTE]
> 🤖 gpt-6.1-sol responding on behalf of Elliot

`gh pr create --attach` rejects a fork contribution with `attaching files requires write access to the repository` when the authenticated user can create the PR but cannot write to its base repository. The user does have admin access to the fork. `--dry-run --attach` is also unsupported, so it cannot publish an attachment preview against the writable fork for reuse in the upstream PR.

Please provide a supported attachment path for fork contributors (for example, select the writable head repository as attachment scope), or explain the limitation and a supported fallback in the command help. At present the help describes attachment uploads without stating the base-repository write requirement.

Observed with gh 2.100.0 on Windows. No tokens, paths, or private data are needed to reproduce this permission mismatch.

issue.body:
## Summary

JSON response sanitization changes literal backslash-u text inside a string value, even when that value contains no terminal control character. This silently changes issue body content returned by `gh api` and `gh issue view --json body`. A valid JSON example stored inside a Markdown body can become invalid after readback. The outer API response remains valid JSON; this report concerns its changed string value, not a failure to parse that outer response.

## Steps to reproduce

Run the following Python 3 script with the tested release on `PATH`. It serves only a local fixture, uses an isolated configuration directory and a dummy token, and creates no GitHub resource. The `body` field contains a JSON string example made of ordinary printable text; `control` separately contains an actual ESC character as a sanitization control.

```python
import http.server
import json
import os
import subprocess
import tempfile
import threading

fixture = {"body": '"\\u001b[31mexample"', "control": "\x1b[31mexample", "plain": "example"}
payload = json.dumps(fixture).encode()

class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(payload)
    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass

server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
thread = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
thread.start()
try:
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as config:
        env = {k: v for k, v in os.environ.items() if not k.startswith(("GH_", "GITHUB_"))}
        env.update(GH_CONFIG_DIR=config, GH_TOKEN="local-fixture-placeholder", NO_COLOR="1")
        result = subprocess.run(["gh", "api", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/fixture"], env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        actual = json.loads(result.stdout)
        print("input:", repr(fixture["body"]))
        print("output:", repr(actual["body"]))
        print("body equal:", actual["body"] == fixture["body"])
        print("actual ESC neutralized:", actual["control"] == "^[[31mexample")
        print("plain unchanged:", actual["plain"] == fixture["plain"])
        json.loads(fixture["body"])
        try:
            json.loads(actual["body"])
        except json.JSONDecodeError as error:
            print("embedded JSON:", error.msg)
finally:
    server.shutdown()
    server.server_close()
    thread.join()
```

The fixture was reduced from a public issue body and executed locally. The same failure was also reproduced by fetching the existing issue through both affected commands and comparing its decoded body with a direct REST response. No issue write is necessary to reproduce it.

## Expected behavior

Preserve literal `\u001b` text that is already escaped in the outer JSON string. Decoding that outer string produces printable backslash-u notation, not an ESC character. Keep neutralizing actual control characters, as demonstrated by the separate `control` field.

This distinction matches the [review requirement on the original sanitization change](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/6916#issuecomment-1409101560): already escaped Unicode codepoints should remain unchanged. It also matches the sanitizer's stated scope: bytes that are not part of a control character are not modified. This report does not assume that `gh api` generally bypasses sanitization or preserves the entire wire response byte for byte.

## Actual behavior

Both the installed executable and a separately downloaded official release executable produced the following result with stdout captured through a pipe and color disabled. Each command exited successfully. The source body and its embedded JSON parse successfully; the returned body's embedded JSON does not.

```text
input: '"\\u001b[31mexample"'
output: '"\\^[[31mexample"'
body equal: False
actual ESC neutralized: True
plain unchanged: True
embedded JSON: Invalid \escape
```

The two `repr` lines above display a Python representation of the strings. The replacement leaves a literal backslash before caret notation. Adding `--allow-escape-sequences` did not preserve the value, and `--jq .body` returned the same changed text. Actual ESC sanitization and ordinary text preservation both passed the controls.

## Evidence

- Expected source: The original change's review requirement linked above and [`asciisanitizer.Sanitizer.Transform`'s documented scope](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/asciisanitizer/sanitizer.go#L27-L29) distinguish actual control characters from other bytes.
- Failure source: The executed self-contained fixture and output above, reproduced with both release executables; an independent live REST comparison also showed five literal escape tokens changed in a stored issue body while GitHub retained the original content.
- Evidence provenance: observed
- Local verification: reproduced
- Reproduction completeness: complete

The HTTP response path applies the [JSON sanitizer to application/json responses](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/api/http_client.go#L259-L273). The [matching branch](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/asciisanitizer/sanitizer.go#L69-L94) recognizes the six-byte escape pattern even after an escaped backslash. Its extra-backslash handling keeps the outer JSON valid, but still changes the decoded literal text. This is a source explanation, not a prescribed implementation.

There is counterevidence worth making explicit: the current [sanitizer test](https://github.com/cli/go-gh/blob/v2.17.0/pkg/asciisanitizer/sanitizer_test.go#L24-L29) and the CLI's [HTTP client test](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/eeb44bc432c0107de002dadd34a61b4e2bd15882/api/http_client_test.go#L431-L471) encode the existing replacement for escaped patterns. They protect outer-JSON validity but do not preserve the printable literal value. The narrower failure here is the content change demonstrated above, rather than a request to remove control-character protection.

## Restoration check

With the same fixture, the returned `body` must equal the input `body`, and `json.loads(actual["body"])` must succeed as it does for the input. The `control` field must still contain caret notation rather than an actual ESC character, and `plain` must remain unchanged. Check both direct API output and issue-body structured output so that a passing outer JSON parse alone cannot hide the content change.

## Runtime or environment

- Runtime-tested: GitHub CLI 2.103.3 on macOS arm64, both the installed Mach-O executable and the official macOS arm64 release archive; the archive's SHA-256 matched the published checksums. All output was captured without a TTY.
- Source-inspected, not built: current default branch `trunk` at `eeb44bc432c0107de002dadd34a61b4e2bd15882`; the HTTP client and its sanitization tests are unchanged from the release. Both pin `github.com/cli/go-gh/v2 v2.17.0`, which was also the library's latest published release when checked.

## References

- [Closed issue #8336](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/8336) concerned invalid outer JSON causing issue view to fail; its fix restored parseability. This report reproduces changed string content while the outer response remains parseable.
- [Closed issue #14545](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/14545) was not reproduced and was closed requesting exact current reproduction; it alleged backslash loss and invalid outer JSON. This report provides a current local fixture for a different observable result and makes no user-agent-dependent or reserialization claim.

## Triage assessment

- Impact level: P2
- Assessment status: supported
- Impact basis: Structured readback silently changes valid literal source text, making an embedded JSON example invalid and preventing exact issue-body verification; the observed scope is strings containing escaped control-code notation.
- Workaround status: available
- Workaround basis: A direct REST request using Python urllib preserved the decoded issue body and its valid embedded example in the live comparison; this avoids the CLI response sanitizer without changing the stored issue or weakening terminal protection in gh.

issue.body: Releated to #5961 ### Description Added support of 1password to save tokens and refresh tokens, instead of the default location gh auth login --op For security reasons and In corporates especially, it is very important to access the gh token in a secured way We started to work like this, any time we need to access gh token, we use Fingerprint to get it from 1password This way it is not possible to get the token freely when it saved in keychain, and any plugin of VScode or any code running on the machine can get it We build the gh on MAC (we work on MAC only, not tested on Win or Linux) and now use it always like this So the code is saving tokens in 1Password instead of keychain if --op flag is given, and makes it the default Reads the tokens from 1Password and refreshes them to 1Password only --> ### How did you test this change? I use the 1password supported gh I build for 2 weeks now and used it on 2 MAC laptops I use it in everyday work in production with EMU and non EMU organizations at work gh --version gh version 0.0.4-fix-recreate-op-records-if-deleted (2026-10-28) https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/latest gh auth status github.com ✓ Logged in to github.com account ilya_xxxxxx (**1password**) - Active account: true - Git operations protocol: https - Token: gho_************************************ - Expiring token that gh refreshes automatically - Token expires: 2026-11-03T00:20:17Z (in about 8 hours) - Refresh token expires: 2027-05-02T16:20:16Z (in about 6 months) - Token scopes: 'gist', 'read:org', 'repo', 'workflow' ### Key points I work with it only on MAC, but as GH owner in my company the idea is all users will use it in the company And even it will be the default option for all users ### Authorship and follow-up Who wrote this: - [V] A human wrote it. Who answers review comments: - [V] @ilyaro will read and reply directly.

comment.body:
Thanks for the work you've put into this, @ilyaro.

Adding to [Will's thoughts](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/14908#issuecomment-6584938094), I don't think we should couple gh's authentication to a specific password manager. This reaches beyond storing a token: login, token refresh, logout, and error handling would all carry 1Password-specific behavior for us to maintain.

A more general interface could avoid that coupling, but it brings its own challenges. We'd need to work through the security implications of delegating credential handling to external programs, including how access is authorized and failures are handled. That needs a design discussion across different stores and platforms before we commit to supporting an interface.

I'm going to close this PR rather than ask you to keep investing in an implementation before we've agreed on an approach. As Will suggested, please open an issue describing your use case so we can discuss the requirements separately from this implementation.
